newsitem.title: USA: Waste towns ask Massachusetts lawmakers for funds.
newsitem.headline: Waste towns ask Massachusetts lawmakers for funds.

text.p: Lawmakers from communities in the Northeast Solid Waste Committee (NESWC) asked Massachusetts to help defray the costs of cleaning up air pollution at their North Andover waste-to-energy site, State House News Service said.

At a Wednesday hearing of the Natural Resources Committee, Kevin Foley, chairman of the Board of Selectmen in Andover, called the NESWC agreement "probably the worst public contract in the United States."

NESWEC dates back to the early 1980s, when the state began threatening to shut down unlined landfills, said Sen. Susan Fargo, D-Lincoln. Fargo, then a newspaper editor in Lincoln, said the 23 NESWC communities were pressured by the state into building a waste-to-energy site in North Andover.
In exchange for financing the construction of the site, which converts garbage to electricity, the communities were promised 89.5 percent of the revenues from the sale of electricity.

According to Fargo, "well-meaning state officials made false assumptions," predicting that the cost of electricity would rise and NESWC towns would quickly be able to pay off the debt from the plant's construction.

Instead, electricity prices fell. The plant brought in little revenue, and communities were left with a high construction bill, now exacerbated by the expense of bringing the plant up to speed with the 1995 Clean Air Act.

Rep. Barry Finegold, D-Andover, said the cost of compliance with the Clean Air Act would make the budget for waste disposal four times as high in NESWC towns as the state average. "The state was the one who got these communities into this," Finegold said, urging passage of a bill establishing a grant for reimbursing the costs of the air pollution renovations.

The committee also heard testimony on a bill incorporating wetlands stewardship into the wetlands protection act. Dr. Jerome Carr, at whose request the bill was filed, believes restrictions are too great on preserving wetlands.
Opponents, from the Massachusetts Audubon Society to the Department of Environmental Protection, said they believed the bill would remove necessary safeguards.
